A shortcoming is a fault or weakness — specifically, a way in which someone or something falls short of a standard, expectation, or ideal.

The word itself carries its meaning inside it: falling short of where you should have come. Something has a shortcoming when it was expected to reach a certain level but didn't quite get there.
A Simple Definition

A shortcoming is a gap between what something is and what it should or could be.

That gap — that failure to meet a standard — is the shortcoming.
Examples to Build Intuition

• "His biggest shortcoming as a manager is that he avoids difficult conversations."
    → He should handle conflicts; he doesn't. That gap is the shortcoming.
  • "The report highlighted several shortcomings in the city's water supply system."
    → The system was expected to work properly and safely; it didn't meet that standard in several ways.
  • "The plan was creative, but its main shortcoming was the lack of a realistic budget."
    → A good plan needs a realistic budget. This one didn't have one — that's where it fell short.

Notice that in every case, there is an implied standard — something that should have been there, and wasn't.
What It Feels Like in Tone

"Shortcoming" is a measured, relatively neutral word. It acknowledges a problem without being harshly judgmental or dramatic. When someone says "one of his shortcomings is...", they are being honest and evaluative — but not attacking.

Compare this feeling to other words:

  • Flaw feels sharper, as if there's a crack or defect.
  • Fault often carries blame — it was someone's fault.
  • Failure is more severe — something completely didn't work.
  • Shortcoming is softer. It says: this didn't reach the mark, not this was a disaster.

This is why people often use "shortcoming" when giving balanced criticism — in job performance reviews, academic evaluations, policy analyses, or honest self-reflection. It's serious enough to be meaningful, but measured enough to be fair.
Who or What Can Have Shortcomings?

Almost anything can have a shortcoming, but it must be something that can be held to a standard or expectation:

  • People — "Despite her many strengths, her shortcoming is impatience."
  • Systems or institutions — "The healthcare system has significant shortcomings in rural areas."
  • Plans and ideas — "The proposal has merit, but its shortcomings need to be addressed before approval."
  • Products or designs — "The app's main shortcoming is its slow loading speed."
  • Arguments or theories — "The theory is interesting, but critics have pointed out several shortcomings."

It does not apply well to things that have no standard to be measured against — you wouldn't say "a stone has shortcomings" unless you were judging it against a specific use (e.g., as a building material).
Singular vs. Plural

Both forms are common, but "shortcomings" (plural) is used more frequently in everyday language. This is because when we evaluate something — a person, a plan, a system — we tend to identify multiple weak points rather than just one.

  • "His shortcoming is arrogance." (one specific fault)
  • "His shortcomings include arrogance, poor listening, and impatience." (a cluster of faults)
Key Phrases You'll Encounter

Learning to recognize how "shortcoming" is used in real sentences will help you use it naturally:

  • "Despite its shortcomings..." — acknowledges faults before saying something positive
  • "One of the main shortcomings of..." — pointing to a central weakness
  • "to address / acknowledge / overcome shortcomings" — dealing with weaknesses
  • "personal shortcomings" — a person's own character flaws
  • "the shortcomings of the system/policy/plan" — weaknesses in something larger
How It Differs from Similar Words (The Fine Distinctions)

WordCore flavour
ShortcomingA failure to meet a standard; a gap between what is and what should be
WeaknessA point where strength or ability is low; can be neutral (not always a failure)
FlawAn imperfection, often in a thing; suggests a crack or defect in an otherwise complete whole
FaultOften implies blame or responsibility; "it was his fault"
LimitationA boundary or constraint on what something can do; not always a negative judgment
DeficiencySomething is missing or insufficient; more clinical

Shortcoming sits in the middle of this group — it is evaluative (there is a standard being applied), honest (a problem is being named), but not severe or blame-focused.
A Note on Register (Formality)

"Shortcoming" is semi-formal to formal. You'll see it often in:

  • Written evaluations, reports, and reviews
  • Academic and professional discussions
  • Journalism and analysis
  • Thoughtful, serious conversation

You would not typically use it in very casual speech. You wouldn't say to a friend: "Your shortcoming is you eat too fast." You'd say: "You eat too fast, that's your problem." But in a performance review, a written critique, or a careful discussion, "shortcoming" fits perfectly.
In Summary

A shortcoming is a fault or weakness — a place where someone or something has not measured up to what was expected or required. It is an honest, balanced word that names a gap without being harsh or dramatic. It applies to people, systems, plans, and ideas. It is most at home in thoughtful evaluation and honest self-awareness, and it almost always implies that there was a standard the person or thing was supposed to meet — but didn't, at least not fully.
